rationale: A wins because it gives the founder sharper beat separation and harder proof gates instead of turning every usable fact into a soft comeback profile. Its best angle, "Peloton's churn hit a record low — the number that decides whether the turnaround is real," is a real reporter question; B's "The new CEO cut $200M a year — what got cut, and what it cost" is a management profile built on one cost-cut fact and a pile of missing basics. A nearly loses the room with a bad rental headline, but its refused angles and uncomfortable questions are plainly more useful.
gaps_in_A: "Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them" is false as written. The update says Peloton is expanding rentals nationwide, not that it stopped selling bikes.
"$2,000+ upfront purchase" and "The $2,000 bike" are unsupported by the supplied facts. Source the price or cut it.
The two rental angles overlap: "Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them" and "The $2,000 bike is now a monthly bill" share the same peg and some of the same proof burden.
"first profitable quarter" needs even more caution because the update says positive adjusted EBITDA and free cash flow, while Peloton remains net-unprofitable.
gaps_in_B: "The new CEO cut $200M a year — what got cut, and what it cost" is thin as an exec angle because the set itself admits it still needs the CEO's name, start date, background, quote, and tradeoffs.
"connected-fitness comeback story" smuggles in a broader comeback narrative the update does not prove.
"the once-doubted retention story is improving" invents prior skepticism rather than grounding the angle in the supplied churn fact.
"$1,000+ hardware sale" is an unsupported price claim from outside the update. Smaller sin than A's "stopped selling" line, still a sin.
